{"body":"## Reviewer brief

**Result:** `pnpm --dir apps/obsidian lint:scanner` runs the ESLint config the Obsidian community directory uses to scan every release. Errors block a submission; warnings don't. The blocking rules also show in the editor, and CI fails when a PR adds a line that breaks one. No source files change.

**Why now:** our v1.7.0 scan reported errors we couldn't see locally. Both reproduce with this config at the exact file and line (`useSchemaSelection.ts:117`, `tagNodeHandler.ts:120`).

**Review focus:**

- `packages/eslint-config/obsidian-scanner.upstream.js` is vendored verbatim (MIT) from [obsidianmd/obsidian-workflows](https://github.com/obsidianmd/obsidian-workflows/blob/8167caed39664214d82c86fdfa32e06d8d55f61d/src/lint.ts#L544-L697): the exact output of its `buildScannerEslintConfig()` at commit `8167cae`. Review that it matches upstream rather than reading it line by line. It's in `.prettierignore` so it stays diffable.
- `apps/obsidian/eslint.config.mjs`, the config editors read, derives the blocking rules from the vendored file instead of listing them: every rule at `error`, the plugin instances that define them, and the scanner's ignores, so `scripts/` and tests stay out as they do in the real scan. Re-vendoring a newer upstream updates the editor with no second edit.
- `lint:scanner` runs as a separate config and process because `@repo/eslint-config` loads `eslint-plugin-only-warn`, which patches ESLint on import and forces every rule to `warn`. The main config can therefore only report blockers as warnings, so `.vscode/settings.json` renders them as errors in the editor.
- `.github/workflows/ci.yaml` runs `lint:scanner` through reviewdog with `-filter-mode=added` and `-fail-level=error`, matching `lint-changed-files`.

**Risk and follow-up:**

- The official scan reported 67 ESLint errors at `256ff3be`, this branch's verification base. CI reports existing findings without blocking. Clearing them is ENG-2341, which has since merged to main.
- **Outside ESLint, the official scan reports a manifest error:** `manifest-id-banned-word`, because plugin ID `@discourse-graph/obsidian` contains "obsidian". Changing an existing plugin's ID breaks installs, so this needs a decision separate from this PR.
- The editor shows only the rules that block. Warn-level findings, including `no-console`, appear only in `lint:scanner`. `no-console` doesn't block because the scanner treats it as a warning, even though `apps/obsidian/AGENTS.md` bans it.
- The scanner's stylelint pass isn't mirrored yet; the official run reports 39 stylelint warnings and no stylelint errors on our CSS. Follow-up.
- Our v1.7.0 directory scan reported "Source review dependency installation failed", a [known scanner limitation with pnpm workspaces](https://forum.obsidian.md/t/bug-plugin-scorecard-linter-cannot-resolve-internal-deps-in-monorepos/116176), so `.tsx` files were never scanned there. **Review branch** on the directory entry stays the only real check.
- 10 files is above the five-file guideline. The diff is 268 lines excluding the lockfile, and 151 of those are the vendored config.

## Verification

**Against Obsidian's own scanner code.** I ran the `obsidian-workflows` action itself (`dist/index.js` at `8167cae`, `scanner-lint: true`, `strict: true`) and this PR's `lint:scanner` on a clean checkout of `256ff3be`:

| ESLint findings | errors | warnings |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Official action, strict | 67 | 111 |
| This PR's `lint:scanner` | 68 | 110 |

176 of 178 findings match by file, line, column, rule, and severity. The two differences:

- `postcss.config.js`: both runs hit the same parse failure. The action reports it as a notice and raw ESLint as an error. It's at line 0, so it never lands on an added line and CI is unaffected.
- `fileChangeListener.ts:239`: the action reports one `no-unnecessary-type-assertion` warning that this PR doesn't. The cause is the TypeScript version: the action doesn't pin TypeScript, so npm resolves typescript-eslint's peer to 6.0.3, while this PR uses the repo's 5.5.4. A 2×2 run (typescript-eslint 8.61.1/8.67.0 × TypeScript 5.5.4/6.0.3) reports the warning exactly when TypeScript is 6.0.3. Warning-level, so it doesn't block.

Full traces: [official run](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/pull/1328#issuecomment-6003442469), with the action's step summary and a reproduction command, and [this PR's run with the diff](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/pull/1328#issuecomment-6003442796). `lint:scanner` still reports 67 errors and 111 warnings on `b42221f3`.

**In the editor.** Open the worktree as the workspace; both lines below should show red. Both are errors in the official scan:

- `apps/obsidian/src/components/ModifyNodeModal.tsx:170`: `obsidianmd/no-static-styles-assignment`
- `apps/obsidian/src/components/RelationshipSection.tsx:100`: `eslint-comments/require-description`

**Other checks:**

- CI is green on `b42221f3`.
- The vendored file is byte-identical to upstream's generator output, and the commit hook leaves it unchanged.
- The editor derivation yields the same 20 blocking rules as the earlier hand-written list. Adding the scanner's ignores changed `pnpm lint` output by exactly 5 findings, all in `scripts/`, which `lint:scanner` never reported.
- CI is proven end to end. A pushed commit that planted `el.style.color = "red"` turned `obsidian-scanner-lint` red, and reverting it turned the check green.
- Existing lint is unaffected. `base.js`, `react-internal.js`, and `next.js` are unchanged.

## Loom video

https://www.loom.com/share/6e76713941124e92bc036634fa606c7c

## Scope check

- [x] Ran `$scope-check` against ENG-1832 and the final diff.
- Scope beyond `Done When`: the `obsidian-scanner-lint` CI job. `Done When` asks for errors visible in the IDE and usable by agents, not CI enforcement.
- Required now: without it, nothing stops new blocking errors from landing while ENG-2341 clears the existing ones. It can be deferred if reviewers prefer.
- Anyone affected or consulted: Not documented.
- Decision: Not documented.

## Standards check

- [x] Ran `$dg-pr-adherence-check` against the final diff and PR metadata.

## Local delegated full review

- [x] Ran `$dg-delegated-full-review` against `b42221f3`. No findings.

content.text:
I verified the contested facts rather than just summarizing the thread. Two findings change the shape of the argument, so I'll lead with those.

## Two things that reframe the meeting

**1. `strict: false` is worse than Michael's reading and worse than you argued.** You said it flattens errors into warnings. It's actually destructive: `applyEnforcement` in `src/main.ts:23-46` rewrites the finding *before* anything is reported, and only the rewritten array reaches the annotations and the step summary. There is no JSON/SARIF output and no counts output — only `type`, `validation-passed`, `release-url`. So the pre-downgrade severity survives nowhere. Your objection is correct; you now have the code to prove it instead of asserting it.

**2. But your "the 65 will block the next release" claim is the one without evidence.** Obsidian's own docs say the submission gate is one-time: *"You only need to submit the initial version of your plugin. After your plugin has been published, users can download new releases from GitHub directly from within Obsidian."* `community-plugins.json` holds only id/name/author/description/repo — no version field, no per-release approval. The client reads the version from our repo's `manifest.json` and fetches the matching GitHub release. The install-block sentence ("won't be installable until any errors from the automated review are resolved") sits under Step 4 of the *initial* submission flow. No public doc says it re-arms per release on a live entry. The only documented lever against a published plugin is archiving the entry.

This is exactly what Michael has been asking for three times, and the honest answer is that neither of you can establish it from public docs. It's login-gated.

## The four questions

**Q1 — What evidence establishes which findings actually block our published plugin?**

Separate three gates that have been treated as one:

| Gate | Can it stop a release reaching users? |
|---|---|
| Our CI running the action | No. The directory never reads it. |
| The directory scorecard on a live entry | No documented mechanism. Unconfirmed. |
| Human/automated review at first submission | Yes — but spent in our case. |

The action's own step summary says it outright: *"Passing here does not guarantee directory acceptance."*

Concrete way to settle it before deciding anything else: our entry has **Review branch → Run preview scan**, which scans a branch/tag/SHA with no release. Run it on current `main` and read the scorecard. That gives the authoritative error/warning split on the real published artifact, which is the evidence neither of you has. If it's still ambiguous, ask Obsidian directly.

**Q2 — Official action, drop editor parity, remove the copied config?**

My read: yes to dropping the copied config, but not by putting the action in this repo. The action operates on `GITHUB_WORKSPACE` only — there is no input to point it at a subdirectory, so it can't cleanly target `apps/obsidian` in a Turborepo. Running it in the mirror repo `discourse-graph-obsidian` puts it exactly where the directory actually scans, on the artifact that actually ships. That removes the vendored file, removes the monorepo mismatch, and makes the check meaningful.

Dropping exact editor parity is fine — you've both already agreed. Keep `eslint-plugin-obsidianmd` locally at its own severities for editor feedback.

**Q3 — Should existing findings block adoption?**

They shouldn't, and the strict/non-strict framing is a false binary. Run the action with `strict: true` in a **non-blocking** job (`continue-on-error`) and you keep the full error/warning distinction while nothing is gated on the backlog. Then your existing `lint-changed-files` pattern (`-filter-mode=added`) catches new violations. That gets Michael his maintained upstream config and you your severity signal, without fixing 65 things first.

Worth raising as a risk: forum thread 116176 is still open with no staff reply. In a pnpm monorepo the scanner lints with unresolved workspace types and emits `@typescript-eslint/no-unsafe-*` noise. Those map to `warn`, so they wouldn't fail even under strict — but it's a live upstream bug and an argument for running in the mirror rather than here.

**Q4 — What proves the scan covered `.ts` and `.tsx`, and how do we fail on incomplete coverage?**

The action cannot prove it, and this is its sharpest weakness:

- `validation-passed` is computed purely from `status === 'failed' && severity === 'error'`. Inconclusive and skipped never touch it.
- A summary reading **"Inconclusive"** still emits `validation-passed: true` and exit 0.
- Scanner-lint dependency failures (`scanner-eslint-setup-failed`) are filed as `recommendation` / `inconclusive`, which `strict: true` does not touch. `runScannerEslint` calls `ensureUserDeps` and **discards the return value** — ESLint then runs against unresolved imports with no finding at all.
- Skipped checks produce no annotation, only a summary row.

So coverage has to be asserted on our side: run with `--format json`, assert the file list contains `.tsx` files, and fail on zero or on any `eslint-execution-failure`.

And the root cause is ours, not Obsidian's. The mirror repo ships **no lockfile**, and its `tsconfig.json` is copied byte-identical from here — still `extends "@repo/typescript-config/react-library.json"`, a workspace package `sanitizePackageJsonForMirror` strips from the deps. Its `eslint.config.mjs` still imports `@repo/eslint-config`. That's why the install fails. Making `publish.ts` emit a self-contained tsconfig and eslint config fixes it without waiting on Obsidian. That's the ticket I'd file, and it's more valuable than the `.tsx` include change (which you both already agreed to and which, as you noted, doesn't change the store scan on its own).

## Three corrections to carry into the meeting

- **ENG-2341 did not clear the 67.** It changed 5 files and fixed the two errors the real v1.7.0 scan surfaced (`useSchemaSelection.ts:117`, `tagNodeHandler.ts`). The PR body's "Clearing them is ENG-2341, which has since merged to main" is wrong — a rebase would land near 65, not 0. No ticket exists for the backlog yet.
- **The `manifest-id-banned-word` item can be dropped.** `publish.ts:366-378` rewrites the id to `discourse-graphs` at publish time. The banned word only exists in the repo manifest (`@discourse-graph/obsidian`), never in the published artifact. The PR flags this as needing a separate decision; it doesn't.

Roughly yes on the first half, but both words in your framing are doing damage — the store doesn't *pass* us, and our CI wouldn't *block* them.

## The store isn't passing us, it's failing to look

The scorecard reported **"Source review dependency installation failed."** That's not a pass on the `.tsx` files, it's an admission the scan never read them. Your own measurement is the proof: broken install → errors drop from 65 to 1 and 56 `.tsx` files come back as **notices**, which in the action's model is `status: inconclusive, coverage: unavailable`. Inconclusive never counts as failed and never counts as passed.

That's exactly why Q4 matters. An incomplete scan is currently indistinguishable from a clean one at the gate: `validation-passed` is computed only from `status === 'failed' && severity === 'error'`, so a run whose summary reads "Inconclusive" still emits `validation-passed: true` and exit 0.

## The mechanism

Established, from your own runs: whether `.tsx` files land in the TypeScript program depends on the install succeeding. `include: ["**/*.ts"]` only *seeds* the program; `.tsx` enter transitively because included `.ts` files import them. Working install → they're in the program → all 65 surface. Broken install → they're not → typescript-eslint can't parse them → skipped as notices, every rule on those files silently dropped, including the comment-hygiene ones that aren't type-aware at all.

What I can't yet state as fact is *why* the `.ts` files survived the broken install while `.tsx` didn't. The plausible candidate: the mirror's `tsconfig.json` still extends `@repo/typescript-config/react-library.json`, which isn't published, so `jsx` never gets set and TS can't parse `.tsx` at all — while the `.ts` seed set still lints. Coherent with both observations, but I haven't reproduced it. Worth pinning down, because Q4's answer is "assert on the right signal" and that means knowing which signal actually moves.

## Our CI would not block on the 65

This is where the thread has been talking past itself. Three different surfaces, three different behaviours:

| Surface | Sees the 65? | Blocks? |
|---|---|---|
| Store scan today | No — install fails | No |
| Official action, `strict: true` | Yes, whole repo | **Yes** — no changed-lines filter |
| This PR's `obsidian-scanner-lint` | Yes, reports all | No — `-filter-mode=added`, only new lines fail |

So your Nov-1 comment ("Running the scanner action directly would bring up these 65 → block CI → we need to fully address them all before we can merge any PR") is true of **the official action**, and that's the real cost of Michael's proposal. It is not true of the reviewdog job you actually built, which reports the backlog without gating on it. Michael's Nov-2 reply was making precisely that distinction, and it's correct for your design.

That's the cleanest thing to put in front of him: your PR already solves the "don't block on the backlog" problem that `strict: false` was proposed to solve — and it solves it without destroying the error/warning signal.

## What changes once we fix the install

Fixing the mirror's tsconfig makes the store scan start seeing all 65. At that point the question becomes live, and it's the one nobody has evidence for: *does a scorecard error actually stop an update to an already-published plugin?* The public registry file says installs resolve straight from our GitHub release with no per-release approval. If that holds, the 65 become a quality problem rather than a shipping blocker — which changes how urgently they need clearing, and changes whether Michael's "fix them first, then adopt" sequencing is the right call.

Which argues for running the preview scan **before** deciding the sequencing, not after.
what do you mean by "working install"

Fair pull — I was using it as a single switch when it's at least two separate things, and the difference matters for what you assert in the meeting.

"Working install" was shorthand for: *the project's dependencies are present and resolvable at the moment ESLint builds the TypeScript program.* But in the mirror repo there are two independent defects stacked, and only one of them is what the scorecard reported:

**1. `npm install` itself fails.** The mirror ships no lockfile, and `sanitizePackageJsonForMirror` strips the `workspace:*` deps and pins the rest. That's the failure the scorecard named.

**2. `extends "@repo/typescript-config/react-library.json"` is unresolvable — permanently.** This one is not fixed by making `npm install` succeed. That package is a workspace package, it is not published to npm, and `sanitizePackageJsonForMirror` removes it from the dependency list. So even a *completely clean* `npm install` in the mirror cannot provide it. The tsconfig's `extends` is broken in the published artifact no matter what the installer does.

So "fix the install" is underspecified, and I shouldn't have compressed it. Two fixes are needed, and they're independent.

Why the distinction bears on the `.tsx` question: those two defects would break `.tsx` inclusion by *different* mechanisms. A missing `node_modules` breaks resolution of imported packages — which changes what the type-aware rules *report*, but doesn't obviously remove a locally-imported `.tsx` file from the program, since relative imports don't need `node_modules`. A broken `extends`, on the other hand, means `jsx` never gets set, and then TypeScript can't parse `.tsx` at all — which *would* drop all 56 of them while leaving the `.ts` seed set linting normally.

That second one fits your measurement much better than the first. But it's still the hypothesis I flagged, not something I've reproduced, and it's worth an hour because it determines the answer to Q4. "Prove the scan covered `.ts` and `.tsx`" needs a specific observable to assert on, and right now the candidates point at different assertions:

- if it's the `extends` → assert the resolved `compilerOptions` contain `jsx`, or assert the emitted file list includes `.tsx`
- if it's `node_modules` → assert install exit code, which the action deliberately discards in `runScannerEslint`

"Make `publish.ts` emit a self-contained tsconfig" is the real fix, and it's the one that matters, because it's the defect that survives Obsidian fixing their installer. The forum thread you linked is about their scanner not resolving monorepo internals — but our mirror isn't a monorepo, it's a flat single package. Our `extends` would be broken there even if upstream shipped a perfect fix tomorrow.

content.text:
Almost, but one correction: the store scanner never sees the monorepo. It only scans the published copy, [discourse-graph-obsidian](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph-obsidian), and that copy has no way to get the shared config.

## In simple terms

TypeScript has to be told how to read JSX, the HTML-like syntax inside `.tsx` files. That setting is `jsx`, and in our code it lives in one place only:

- [react-library.json:5](packages/typescript-config/react-library.json:5) contains `"jsx": "react-jsx"`.
- Our plugin's [tsconfig.json:2](apps/obsidian/tsconfig.json:2) doesn't set `jsx` itself. It only says "start from that shared file": `"extends": "@repo/typescript-config/react-library.json"`.

So whether `.tsx` files can be read depends on whether that shared file can be found.

## Why our CI finds it and the store doesn't

**In the monorepo (our CI and your laptop):**
- [apps/obsidian/package.json:24](apps/obsidian/package.json:24) lists `"@repo/typescript-config": "workspace:*"`.
- `pnpm install` turns that into a shortcut (a symlink) on disk. You have it: `apps/obsidian/node_modules/@repo/typescript-config → packages/typescript-config`.
- The `extends` resolves, `jsx` is set, the `.tsx` files get read, and all ~65 errors show up.

**In the published copy (what the store scans):**
- [publish.ts:408-434](apps/obsidian/scripts/publish.ts:408) copies the plugin and removes every `workspace:` dependency. Its comment says why: *"The community review runs npm install with no lockfile, so pnpm-only specifiers fail."*
- The mirror's `package.json` therefore has no `@repo/typescript-config`, and the package isn't on npm, so no install can supply it.
- The mirror's `tsconfig.json` is still an exact copy of ours, `extends` line included. It points at a file that doesn't exist there.

In one line: **our CI has the symlink and the store doesn't.** Same code, same tsconfig, but the shared file only exists inside the monorepo.

The `include: ["**/*.ts"]` setting also plays a part. It only lists `.ts` files directly; `.tsx` files get pulled in because `.ts` files import them. That's why `.tsx` files get linted in CI even though `include` never names them. You described this in your [Nov 2 comment](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/pull/1328#issuecomment-6580132197).

## What's proven and what isn't

**Checked against the code just now:**
- `jsx` is set only in the shared file.
- The mirror's tsconfig extends that file.
- The mirror's `package.json` doesn't include it.
- `publish.ts` removes it on purpose.
- The monorepo has the symlink.

**Measured earlier, by you:** with a broken install, errors went from 65 to 1, and 56 `.tsx` files were skipped as notices. In the action's code, a file ESLint can't parse becomes `eslint-execution-failure`, which is only a notice and never fails the run (`src/lint.ts:294-318` at `8167cae`).

**Not proven:** that the missing `jsx` setting is what causes the skip. I tried to clone the mirror and run the scan here, but the command was declined. There's also a timing question. ENG-2341 ([#1499](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/pull/1499), merged Sept 29) added the `package.json` cleanup, so `npm install` may now succeed on the mirror (currently 1.8.0). If it does, the missing shared config is the only blocker left. The latest scorecard for 1.8.0 would show which: whether it still says "Source review dependency installation failed", and whether any `.tsx` findings appear.

## What this means for the fix

Adding `**/*.tsx` to `include` won't change the store scan, because the `extends` stays broken either way. The fix is in `publish.ts`: write a tsconfig into the mirror that has the shared settings copied in (including `jsx`) instead of the `extends` line. The mirror's `eslint.config.mjs` has the same problem, since it imports `@repo/eslint-config`. Once both are self-contained, the store should start linting the `.tsx` files, and the ~65 errors will show up there too.
why TypeScript has to be told how to read JSX?

Short answer: JSX isn't JavaScript. It's extra syntax that has to be turned into normal function calls before a browser can run it, and there's more than one way to do that. The `jsx` setting tells TypeScript which way.

## What JSX turns into

You write:

```tsx
<Button onClick={save}>Save</Button>
```

There's no `<Button>` in JavaScript, so a tool has to rewrite that line. There are two common ways:

- **Classic** (`"jsx": "react"`): becomes `React.createElement(Button, { onClick: save }, "Save")`. You must have `React` imported in every file.
- **Automatic** (`"jsx": "react-jsx"`, which is ours): becomes `_jsx(Button, { onClick: save, children: "Save" })`, with the import added for you from `react/jsx-runtime`.

There are also modes like `preserve`, which leaves JSX untouched for another tool to handle. TypeScript can't pick for you, because the right choice depends on your React version and your build tool. So JSX is opt-in, and our choice lives in [react-library.json:5](packages/typescript-config/react-library.json:5).

It also affects type-checking: TypeScript checks a component's props using the types of whichever runtime you picked.

## A correction to what I said earlier

I said TypeScript "can't parse `.tsx` at all" without this setting. That's wrong. TypeScript recognises JSX from the `.tsx` file extension and still parses the file. Without `jsx`, it reports a type error on each JSX line: *TS17004: "Cannot use JSX unless the '--jsx' flag is provided."*

typescript-eslint also turns on JSX parsing from the file extension. So a missing `jsx` setting on its own probably would not make ESLint skip the 56 `.tsx` files. That weakens the explanation I gave you.

The broken `extends` is still the likely cause, but through a different route. When the base config file can't be found, TypeScript may fail to load the tsconfig at all, and then the `.tsx` files never get into the set of files ESLint checks. I haven't reproduced it. Running the scan against the mirror is still the only way to know which one it is, so don't present the `jsx` explanation in the meeting as established.

The fix doesn't change: have `publish.ts` write a self-contained tsconfig into the mirror, with no `extends` pointing at a file it can't get.
